clue.text: Oil company restricts identifying images in this place, the world of online opinions

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so the company's letters close around the next word

parts.note: BP is the British oil giant
logos are emblems that identify a brand
here means in this place

explanation.surface: An oil firm hems in its brand images within the online commentary world.
explanation.walkthrough: BLOGOSPHERE is B(LOGOS)P followed by HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: The blogosphere is the collective community of blogs and the commentary they publish on the internet.

clue.text: Underwear provided for piece of the skull

parts.note: a bra is an undergarment
in case can mean provided that, on condition

explanation.surface: An odd scene of underwear supplied for a bit of a skull.
explanation.definitionFit: The braincase is the cranium, the part of the skull enclosing the brain.

clue.text: Only parts to be sadly out of date

indicators.note: to part something is to split it, letting the first word go into the gap
sadly suggests the words have come to grief, so their letters fall into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
sole means only, as in sole survivor

explanation.surface: Only some components are, unhappily, past their use-by date.
explanation.walkthrough: OBTE is the rearranged TO BE, split open by SOLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsolete describes something no longer used or superseded, i.e. outmoded.

clue.text: Wild party is held in outdoor gymnasium

indicators.note: is held in says the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A rowdy bash is staged at an open-air gym.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy is a wild, unrestrained party.

clue.text: Undermine clout and trap one of the Koch brothers, perhaps

definitions.text: one of the Koch brothers, perhaps

indicators.note: to undermine is to subvert and dislodge, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political call to weaken a billionaire's power and ensnare him.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles and David Koch were American billionaires known for funding conservative politics.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is someone whose wealth gives them political power, which is what the Kochs exemplify.

clue.text: Laws cited wrongly by Senate's leader

indicators.note: wrongly cited means quoted incorrectly, so the letters come out in a wrong order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a word's leader is the letter at its front

parts.note: first letter of Senate

explanation.surface: The Senate leader got the statutes he quoted wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Edicts are official decrees issued by an authority, so they serve as laws.

clue.text: Planes are in Haarlem, for example

definitions.meaning: first meaning: levels, makes smooth or flat, a verb in the third person
second meaning, cryptic: the letters in the even positions of the word Haarlem (second, fourth, sixth) spell are

explanation.walkthrough: Haarlem, a flat Dutch city, makes 'Planes' look like aircraft or level land. Take the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of HAARLEM: A, R, E, which is why 'are' is in Haarlem as its evens.
explanation.definitionFit: To even a surface is to level or smooth it, which is exactly what a carpenter's plane does.

clue.text: Initiator of workplace tussle over lunch items

indicators.note: the initiator of something is what starts it, so only the opening letter of workplace counts

parts.note: first letter of workplace

indicators.note: in a down-or-across clue, over means turned over, so the fight word is read from the end back

parts.note: to spar is to tussle or box

explanation.surface: An office scuffle starts over who gets which sandwich at lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: W then SPAR turned round gives WRAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Wraps are tortilla-style sandwiches, a common lunch food.

clue.text: Rudimentary anemometer is loud (if useless)

indicators.note: something said loud is heard rather than read, so the bracketed words are taken by their sound

parts.note: if can mean whether, as in ask if it rains
in vain means to no purpose, so vain is useless

explanation.surface: A crude wind gauge makes plenty of noise but does little.
explanation.walkthrough: Whether vain, said out loud, is the two words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A weather vane shows wind direction, a simple ancestor of the instrument that measures wind.

clue.text: Mathematician accepting homemade periodical's transparency

indicators.note: someone accepting a thing takes it in, so the scientist's name wraps around the magazine word

parts.note: Carl Friedrich Gauss, the German mathematician
a zine is a self-published, homemade magazine

explanation.surface: A mathematician takes in a fanzine and admires how see-through it is.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's is part of the surface: GAU(ZINE)SS.
explanation.definitionFit: Gauze is a thin, sheer fabric, so gauziness is a sheer, see-through quality.

clue.text: Tyne Daly's costar and lead in Hunter admitted to going naked in Malaysia?

indicators.note: admitted to means let inside, so the single letter goes into the phrase that follows

parts.note: a sarong is the wrap worn in Malaysia, so without one you would be bare

indicators.note: the lead in a word is its front letter

parts.note: first letter of Hunter

explanation.surface: A trivia question about an actress, with a Malaysian joke tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyne Daly and Sharon Gless co-starred in the 1980s US police show Cagney & Lacey. 'Going naked in Malaysia?' looks like the definition; it is the invented word SARONG-LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharon Gless played Christine Cagney opposite Tyne Daly's Mary Beth Lacey on television.

clue.text: Ronald: bad actor and governor

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters of the name have gone wrong and need putting into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: It reads as a dig at Ronald Reagan, the film actor who became governor of California.
explanation.walkthrough: Reagan is the obvious answer but the wrong one: a different Hollywood star also governed California, Arnold Schwarzenegger.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Schwarzenegger was a film star who later served as governor of California.

clue.text: Sheraton polluted a body of water

indicators.note: something polluted is spoiled and disturbed, so the hotel name's letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hotel chain has dumped waste into nearby waters.
explanation.definitionFit: The North Sea is an arm of the Atlantic between Britain and Scandinavia.

clue.text: Can make it haler, eh?!

indicators.note: can make suggests the words are raw material that may be built into something new

parts.note: the letters of the three words, taken together

explanation.surface: A tin of something is promoted as making you haler, that is, healthier.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the letters of IT HALER EH can be made into HEALTHIER, and the clue also says a can of something makes you haler.
explanation.definitionFit: Hale means robust and well, so haler is a dated synonym for in better condition.

clue.text: Characteristic of lamb on ice, with ingredients chopped up and reused

indicators.note: chopping up a recipe's ingredients mixes them, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the clue's own ingredients used again: three of the five letters of on ice repeated, one of them twice
says the fodder letters come back for a second use

explanation.surface: A recipe note for lamb on ice, with the ingredients diced up and used again.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is unusual: the five letters of ON ICE supply every letter of the answer, but N, C and E must be used more than once, which is what 'reused' admits.
explanation.definitionFit: The lamb is a traditional symbol of innocence, its defining quality in poetry and scripture.

clue.text: Therefore, monster returns

indicators.note: something that returns goes back the way it came, so the creature is read backwards

parts.note: an ogre is a monster of folklore

explanation.surface: A horror-film line: and so the creature comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is the Latin-derived connective meaning consequently.

clue.text: Spooner's principal gardener is someone who brings in business

indicators.note: named after the Rev. Spooner, who swapped the opening sounds of word pairs

parts.note: principal is main and a gardener is a raker; swap their opening sounds

explanation.surface: The head gardener is the one who drums up trade.
explanation.definitionFit: In business slang a rainmaker is a person who wins lucrative clients or deals.

clue.text: Unusually clean pet is a magical symbol

indicators.note: unusually signals the letters appear in an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A surprisingly tidy pet is like a lucky charm.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentacle is a five-pointed star used as an occult or magical emblem.

clue.text: Regretted speaker's boorish…

indicators.note: a speaker's version of a word is how it sounds out loud, not how it is written

parts.note: boorish means rude, and the answer sounds identical

explanation.surface: Read with the next clue, someone regrets a speaker's boorish ranting.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue is to feel sorry about, so the past tense means felt sorrow over.

clue.text: …blather and rant: "Get in buggy"

indicators.note: buggy means full of glitches, so the quoted letters come out scrambled

parts.note: the letters of rant and get in, taken together

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: someone's blathering rant ordering people into a carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: Buggy looks like a pram or carriage to climb into; it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Nattering is idle, chatty talk, the same thing as blather.

clue.text: Hero allowed in an apartment arrangement

parts.note: a hero is an American long sandwich, also called a sub
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A hero is permitted to stay in someone's flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Hero means the sandwich, not a brave person.
explanation.definitionFit: A sublet is a deal in which a tenant rents their flat on to someone else.

clue.text: Two air conditioners outside nearly draw oxygen in seaside resort

indicators.note: outside says one of the cooling units sits around the trimmed word

parts.note: AC is short for air conditioner, twice over

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter of the pulling word is dropped

parts.note: to draw is to pull
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: At a beach hotel, a pair of AC units barely manage to pull in any air.
explanation.definitionFit: Acapulco is a famous beach resort city on Mexico's Pacific coast.

clue.text: For instance, Michael Lange is in distress

indicators.note: being in distress means being in a bad state, so the surname's letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An example of someone named Michael Lange in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Lange looks like one person's name; Michael is the archangel and Lange the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael is an archangel in Jewish, Christian and Islamic tradition, so he is an example of a heavenly being.

clue.text: Hinder a redesign of my site

indicators.note: a redesign reorganises the pieces of what was there into a new layout

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A web owner complains that reworking the site slowed things down.
explanation.definitionFit: To stymie is to obstruct or thwart, so it can stand in for hinder.

clue.text: A continent like Iowa

parts.note: as means like, in the same way
IA is the US postal abbreviation for Iowa

explanation.surface: Someone says a continent is like an American Midwestern state.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the largest of the world's continents.

clue.text: Vegetables, for example, with green bottoms containing a bit of lycopene

indicators.note: containing says the trousers word holds the small piece inside it

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
G is a standard abbreviation for green
pants, in American usage, are trousers, worn on the bottom half

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here just its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of lycopene

explanation.surface: A nutrition note about vegetables with green ends and a little of the tomato pigment lycopene.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants here is the American word for trousers; EG, G, then P(L)ANTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggplants are aubergines, the purple fruit cooked and eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Accompaniment for ale or sack, surprisingly involving fifth of booze

indicators.note: surprisingly hints at an unexpected outcome, so the bag's letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the fifth of a word is the letter in fifth place, counting from the start

parts.note: fifth letter of booze

explanation.surface: A pub question: what goes with ale, or with sack, the old fortified wine?
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is an old word for sherry-like wine, which makes the surface feel like a drinks list. The pairing comes from Twelfth Night: 'cakes and ale'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cakes and ale is a stock phrase for carefree pleasures, cakes being ale's traditional companion.

clue.text: Writer of trash took in an ancient city

parts.note: litter is trash dropped in public
to take food in is to eat
Ur was an ancient Sumerian city

explanation.surface: A hack who writes rubbish is taken in by a historic city.
explanation.walkthrough: Writer of trash sounds like one phrase for a hack; only Writer is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A littérateur is a literary person, someone who writes professionally.
